The Lateran Settlement. The Lateran Treaty established Vatican City in 1929 and resolved the Roman Question. Its agreement with fascist Italy is an essential part of the political context.
Manuscript Stewardship. Manuscript stewardship depends on preservation, description, and scholarly access. The library's long history must not be collapsed into the much younger history of the state.

Museum Conservation. Museum conservation brings technical work to inherited collections. It can preserve objects while also prompting difficult questions about acquisition, interpretation, and whose histories are represented.
Scholarly Catalogues. Catalogues make collections discoverable and usable. Their labor is less monumental than palace building but fundamental to sustained historical and scientific research.

Radio and Communications. Modern communications and treaty-guaranteed transport access supported the new state's practical independence. They did not restore the territorial extent or governmental structure of the Papal States.

Cultural Custodianship. Custodianship here means sustained cultural work, not a claim of uncontested moral authority. The kit deliberately offers no settlement-cap bonus or historical rationale for conquest.
Lagoon Communities. Lagoon communities depended on waterborne movement and local ecological knowledge. Their development preceded the fully formed maritime republic.
Arsenal Labor. Arsenal work joined specialized crafts with state demands. Its celebrated efficiency changed over time and relied on a large laboring population.
Fondaco Commerce. Fondachi facilitated and regulated merchant activity. Access to commerce could coexist with close supervision and unequal treatment.
Convoy Contracts. Convoys coordinated shipping, investment, and protection. Commercial success remained exposed to war, piracy, weather, and political bargaining.
Lagoon Stewardship. Managing channels and building sites linked urban growth with environmental consequences. The lagoon was an active working landscape, not merely a defensive moat.
Maritime Dominion. Overseas dominion connected ports but subjected communities to unequal rule. Venice's commercial history cannot be separated from imperial coercion.
Delegation Networks. The delegation that gave the Wafd its name sought to carry Egypt's case abroad. Arrests and exile helped transform that demand into mass mobilization.

The 1923 Constitution. The 1923 constitution created representative institutions while preserving royal powers. Its suspension and restoration demonstrate how precarious constitutional government remained.

Nile Smallholders. Agricultural communities supplied the wealth and population behind national politics. Land concentration and unequal rural conditions complicated claims that independence alone would secure social justice.

Independent Newspapers. Newspapers made constitutional disputes and nationalist arguments public. Their editors and readers faced censorship, partisan conflict, and the power of both palace and occupation.
Provincial Associations. Provincial networks gave the Wafd reach beyond Cairo. Organization depended on local notables and associations as well as popular enthusiasm.
Parliamentary Coalition. Coalitions and electoral victories operated within an uneven balance among party, king, and Britain. The settlement of 1936 did not eliminate that triangular contest.
Plateau Husbandry. Cattle and crops underpinned wealth and subsistence. Imported luxuries should not obscure the importance of everyday agricultural work.
Stoneworking Knowledge. Dry-stone construction demanded skilled labor and material knowledge. Monumental walls expressed local achievement rather than outside colonization.
Gold Routes. Gold moved through inland exchanges to coastal commercial networks. The precise mechanisms of royal involvement are not fully recoverable.
Enclosed Residences. Enclosures organized access and displayed distinctions within settlement. Their functions changed, and some interpretations remain contested.
Indian Ocean Connections. Beads and imported ceramics connect plateau centers with Indian Ocean commerce. Much of that contact operated through regional intermediaries.
Plateau Centers. Khami and other successors transformed inherited traditions. They were not simply unchanged extensions of Great Zimbabwe under different site names.

Chahar Suq. Chahar Suq is an attested name associated with Herat's central bazaar crossroads and cistern complex. The quarter extends that commercial setting to workshops and exchange for gameplay. It does not claim that every Afghan town had an identical district, that its institutions began in the nineteenth century, or that replication is literal.

Caliphal Kasbah. A kasbah could concentrate political residence, military security, and administrative functions within a city. Almohad projects at Marrakesh provide an important setting for this idea. Caliphal Kasbah does not imply that all western Islamic citadels were Almohad inventions or followed one identical internal plan.

Dwabrem. Dwabrem names a gathering space associated with Asante royal ceremony, attested in current Manhyia Palace usage. The quarter extends that ceremonial association to Kumasi's earlier courtly networks. It is not a claim that the present palace, built in 1925, existed throughout the eighteenth century.

Yan. Yan is an attested Thai term for a neighborhood or district, used in historical discussions of Ayutthaya's trading and production areas. This quarter evokes communities linked by waterways and commerce. The local term does not impose a modern administrative ward or claim an identical layout for every neighborhood.

Ceremonial Precinct. Major ceremonial precincts combined temples, open spaces, schools, and facilities connected with ritual authority. The Tenochtitlan precinct developed through repeated construction. Ceremonial Precinct groups these functions without assuming that every altepetl copied the capital's scale or shared an identical arrangement of sacred buildings.

Istinaf. Istinaf names the appellate institution documented among the Ayt Atta, associated with Igherm Amazdar. Its attested name anchors the quarter's arbitration theme. Replication is a gameplay abstraction, not evidence that every Amazigh society shared this court or belonged to a unified national administrative system.

Pátio Ferroviário. Pátio Ferroviário is a descriptive Portuguese label for a railway yard, not the proper name of a standardized historical district. Linking it with research abstracts infrastructure and technical expertise. Export priorities and concentrated ownership shaped rail development, so the quarter does not imply universally shared modernization or benefits.

Augustaion. Augustaion names the enclosed open space south of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, joining important ceremonial and administrative settings. Its form and use changed over time. The historical place name replaces a generic forum label without making every Byzantine city a copy of the capital's center.

Mercado cibaeño. Mercado cibaeño is a descriptive Spanish label meaning a Cibao market, combining attested words rather than naming a historical civic authority. Regional towns joined agricultural exchange with public associations and political interests. The quarter abstracts these connections without claiming one standard plan, equal participation, or cultural uniformity across the republic.

Palatium. Palatium is an attested Latin designation for a Carolingian royal palace, including centers such as Attigny. Residence, assembly, worship, and access to estate resources could coincide there. Rulers moved among such places, and the term does not make every palatium a permanently occupied modern capital.

Cabildo. Cabildo names the municipal council inherited from Spanish American government, whose functions included markets, taxation, and local regulation. Independence transformed rather than erased this institutional landscape. The quarter abstracts civic administration without claiming that all residents enjoyed equal representation or that republican cities adopted one standardized plan.

Kominote. Kominote is the Haitian Creole word for community, used functionally rather than presented as a formally chartered historical district. Households, cultivation, shared obligations, and cultural practice made independence tangible alongside state monuments. The quarter does not imply that rural life lacked hierarchy, conflict, or pressure from government.

Városnegyed. Városnegyed is the Hungarian word for a town quarter or neighborhood, used as a functional label rather than an attested Danube district title. The combination links milling, scholarship, and civic culture in the growing capital without suggesting that metropolitan prosperity characterized every community in the kingdom.

Acropolis Ward. At major fortified settlements, elevated or prominently situated precincts could concentrate elite residences and ritual buildings. Acropolis Ward is an analytical gameplay label for that concentration, not an attested Iberian administrative term or a claim that every town copied a Greek constitution.

Bandar. Bandar is an Indonesian word for a harbor or trading port town. Used as a functional quarter label, it joins maritime exchange with the circulation of students, publications, and political ideas. It does not name a uniform historical institution or erase ports' roles in colonial extraction and coerced labor.

Järmeñke. Järmeñke is the Kazakh word for a fair or market, used as a functional label rather than a particular administrative district title. Exchange could bring performance, news, and negotiation together. The quarter does not turn mobile life into an exclusively urban culture or imply one centralized government for every gathering.

Shahristan. Shahristan is an attested Persian urban term for the inner city, distinguished from outer settlement in descriptions of Central Asian towns. The quarter evokes Gurganj's inhabited commercial core, not a recovered named district. Its surviving monuments span several periods rather than one intact Anushteginid construction program.
Camp Circle. Camp Circle evokes the social and spatial organization of a mobile gathering. It does not turn a tipi camp into an urban quarter or reproduce sacred ceremonial designs.

Gastaldaga. Gastaldaga is the conventional local name for the Cividale area associated with the gastald's administrative setting and the surviving Lombard Tempietto. It replaces a generic English ward label without claiming that every town possessed an identically organized district or that all surviving structures share one date.

Palisaded Village. Palisades surrounded many ancestral Mohawk villages, sometimes in multiple rows. Longhouses and working areas occupied the enclosed space. Palisaded Village represents an inhabited community rather than a purely military installation, and defensive arrangements changed as settlements moved and relations with neighbors shifted.
Household Cluster. Household Cluster represents relationships among nearby homes and working places. It is not an attested Navajo urban administrative district.

Chieftain Farmstead. Differences in house size, grave wealth, and access to imported goods indicate social hierarchies at many northern sites. Chieftain Farmstead is a cautious interpretation of elite households. The label does not recover an attested title or establish that every prominent farm exercised territorial government.

Curia Romana. Curia Romana is the established Latin name for the institutions assisting papal government, whose organization developed substantially over time. The quarter spatially abstracts that administrative setting, including responsibilities beyond territorial rule. It is neither modern Vatican City projected backward nor proof of uniform control over provincial communes.

Royal Enclosure. Rhynie combines enclosure evidence, exceptional metalworking, imported objects, and a suggestive place name. Together these support an interpretation as an important royal center. Royal Enclosure evokes that case without claiming that every Pictish stronghold had the same layout or degree of political authority.

Ribeira. Ribeira names Porto's historic riverside area, where dense urban life developed around exchange and the Douro. Its Portuguese place-name replaces a generic riverside quarter. Replication abstracts related functions elsewhere rather than claiming identical districts or presenting the wider Atlantic economy as free of colonial coercion.

Detinets. Detinets conventionally denotes a fortified inner urban area associated with important residences and institutions. Its form varied considerably between cities. The quarter evokes this defended core without equating it with a later stone Muscovite kremlin or assuming all Rus settlements possessed monumental masonry defenses.

Burgh. Burgh is an attested Scots municipal term for a chartered town with civic privileges, not an invented translation of an industrial district. The quarter combines urban institutions with engineering and learning for gameplay. It does not imply a standardized plan, equal political access, or universally shared industrial prosperity.

Royal Encampment. Elite burial evidence and outside accounts suggest powerful households able to mobilize followers, animals, and wealth. Royal Encampment models that concentration of authority. It is not the reconstructed capital of a documented centralized bureaucracy or proof of a single Scythian court shared across Eurasia.

Chahar Su. Chahar su is an attested Persian expression for a four-way intersection, associated with markets along intersecting streets in Iranian and Central Asian urban descriptions. The quarter models that commercial setting, not a standardized Seljuk administrative ward or a specific securely reconstructed street plan in every listed city.

Skupština. Skupština is the Serbian assembly term used here for civic gathering and representation. Nineteenth-century assemblies operated amid conflict over princely authority and constitutional powers. The quarter abstracts these functions; it does not claim a standardized historical district plan or equal participation by every resident.

Bruk. Bruk is a Swedish term associated with industrial works and the communities around them. Historical works sometimes supported schools, linking education to employers and production. This quarter abstracts that relationship without idealizing paternalism, child labor, or the unequal distribution of power within an industrial settlement.

ʻĀpoʻoraʻa. ʻĀpoʻoraʻa is an attested Tahitian assembly term, used here as a functional gathering-place label rather than a particular royal institution's title. Chiefly households and political audiences shaped changing royal centers. The abstraction does not project the modern territorial legislature unchanged into the Pōmare monarchy or reconstruct a fixed district.

Yucayeque. Yucayeque is a conventional rendering for a Taíno village or settlement. Houses and open gathering spaces formed a lived community rather than a purely ceremonial monument. The quarter uses the documented term cautiously, since spellings and the scale of settlements described in colonial sources vary.

Riverbank Settlement. Archaeological settlement traces along the river reveal occupation, food preparation, pottery, and changing population patterns. Riverbank Settlement deliberately avoids a reconstructed royal or religious title. Its plain English name does not assert a standardized indigenous administrative district or an empire governing all Orinoco communities.

Odrysian Residence. Seuthopolis combined a planned urban setting with a royal residence and religious space. Its archaeology offers unusually concrete evidence for Hellenistic Thracian kingship. Odrysian Residence draws on this conjunction while avoiding the claim that earlier dispersed royal courts had identical monumental layouts.

Registan. Registan is the historical name of Samarkand's prominent square, associated with Ulugh Beg's Timurid madrasa and changing urban activity. The quarter evokes its earlier learned and public setting. It does not assign the entire surviving architectural ensemble to the Timurids; major neighboring madrasas belong to later dynasties.

Cortile del Belvedere. Cortile del Belvedere names the historic courtyard ensemble linking papal spaces and later museum functions. It predates the modern state by centuries. The quarter uses its attested Italian name to connect scholarship and collections, not to designate a new administrative district or another independent city.

Fondamenta. Fondamenta is the Venetian term for a street running beside a canal at the foot of buildings. Such waterfronts connected residences, workshops, landings, and commerce. The attested local word names an urban form rather than a standardized administrative ward or a single master-planned mercantile district.

Bayt al-Umma. Bayt al-Umma, the House of the Nation, was Saad Zaghloul's Cairo residence and a meeting place associated with nationalist politics. Its attested name replaces a generic forum. Treating the house as a repeatable quarter is a gameplay abstraction, not evidence of multiple historical residences.

Zimbabwe Enclosure. Stone enclosures formed only part of a much larger inhabited landscape containing domestic structures and working spaces. Zimbabwe Enclosure evokes the concentration of authority and display within that setting. It does not imply that every resident lived inside a monumental stone-walled palace.

Piyāda-nizām. Piyāda-nizām is a functional Persian/Dari infantry label, not a newly invented Afghan regiment title. Rulers and local forces combined regular troops, retainers, and community mobilization in changing ways. Generic native models approximate firearm-equipped infantry without imposing one uniform, one command, or an exclusively martial identity on Afghan society.

River Pilot represents this expertise at the junction of inland and maritime movement. It is not a named bureaucratic rank or a claim that every route was navigable year-round.

These skills differed between regions. The guide joins them for exploration gameplay without claiming a unified scout corps or making every Amazigh community simultaneously mountain pastoralist and Saharan caravan trader.

Recruitment also involved coercion and unequal obligations, despite the title. Native infantry does not reconstruct their uniforms; later tiers abstract subsequent forces rather than extending one wartime organization unchanged into the republic.

Kataphraktos. Kataphraktos refers to a heavily equipped cavalryman, but the term and associated formations changed across Byzantine history. Military manuals describe specialized arrangements that were not universal across the army. The unit evokes armored mounted combat without turning every imperial horseman into the same elite formation.

Journalists and party organizers traveled through networks rather different from military reconnaissance. The Correspondent turns those connections into exploration gameplay and should not be read as an official Wafdist scout unit.
